source_text: 1. Post haee iam ordo deposcit nos etiam de anima generaliter inquirere et ab inferioribus incipientes ad superiora conscendere. Esse namque animas in singulis quibusque animalibus, etiam in his quae in aquis degunt, a nullo arbitror dubitari. Nam et communis hoc omnium servat opinio, et confirmatio sanctae scripturae auctoritatis accedit, cum dieitur quia “fecit deus cetos magnos et omnem animam animantium repentium, quae produxerunt aquae secundum genus eorum”. Ex communi vero rationis intellegentia confirmatur etiam ab his, qui definitionem animae certis determinant verbis. Definitur 2) namque anima hoe modo, quia sit substantia et quod latine, licet non tam proprie explanetur, diei tamen potest ‘sensibilis et mobilis. Quod utique eonvenit etiam de omnibus animalibus diei et his, quae in aquis degunt; sed et im volueribus eadem definitio animae convenienter ostenditur. Addit sane scriptura etiam alterius sententiae auctoritatem, cum dicit: “Non manducabitis sanguinem, quia anima totius carnis sanguis eius est, et non manducabitis animam cum carnibus”; in quo evidentissime ‘sanguinem’ omnium animalium -animam- ipsorum esse designat. lam vero si quis requirat, quoniam "animam omnis carnis sanguinem eius esse- dixit, de apibus et vespis et formicis sed et de his, quae in aquis sunt, ostreis vel cocleis et quaecumque sunt alia, quae carent sanguine et esse animantia manifestissime demonstrantur: respondendum est quoniam in huiuscemodi animantibus quam in ceteris vim habet rubri sanguinis vigor, hanc vim obtinet in istis humor ille, qui inest in eis, licet alterius sit coloris: nihil enim refert, qui sit color, dummodo substantia sit vitalis. De iumentis vero vel pecudibus quod animantia sint, etiam apud communem opinionem nulla dubitatio est. Evidens tamen est et scripturae divinae sententia, cum dicit deus: “Producat terra animam vivam secundum genus, quadrupedia et repentia et bestias terrae secundum genus”, Iam vero de homine quamvis nulh dubium sit nec requirere aliquis possit, tamen et seriptura divina designat quod “deus in faciem eius inspiraverit spiramentum vitae, et factus sit homo in animam vivam”. Superest de angelico ordine requirere, utrum et ipsi animas habeant an animae sint, vel de ceteris divinis caelestibusque virtutibus sed et de contrarus potestatibus. Auctoritatem ”quidem scripturae divinae nusquam ullam invenimus quod vel angeli, vel si qui sunt divini ‘spiritus ministri. dei, vel animas habere vel animae dicantur; animantia tamen esse a quam plurimis sentiuntur. De deo autem invenimus scriptum esse ita: “Et ponam animam meam super animam illam, quae manducaverit sanguinem, et eradicabo eam de populo suo” et item alibi: “Neomenias vestras et sabbata et diem magnum acceptum non habeo. leiunia et ferias et dies festos vestros odit anima mea”. Et in vicesimo primo psalmo de Christo (certum est enim quia ex persona ipsius iste psalmus adscribitur, sieut. evangelium contestatur) ita dietum est: “Tu autem, domine, ne longe facias auxilium. tuum, ad defensionem meam respice, eripe a framea animam meam et de manu canis unieam meam”. Quamvis et multa alia sint testimonia de anima Christi in carne positi. 2. Sed de Christi quidem anima omnem nobis adimet quaestionem ratio inearnationis occurrens. Siecut enim vere carnem habuit, ita vere et animam habuit. De eo vero, quod ‘dei anima- in scripturis nominatur, quahter intellegi debeat, et sentire et proferre difficile est; semel enim simplicem illam naturam et absque ullius adiectionis permixtione profitemur; tamen, quoquomodo sentiendum est, nominari interim ‘dei anima- videtur: de Christo vero nec dubitatur. Et ideo non mihi videtur absurdum etiam de sanctis angelis ceterisque caelestibus virtutibus tale aliquid. vel dicere vel sentire, si quidem definitio illa animae etiam 1n ipsos videtur incurrere. Quis enim rationabiliter sensibiles eos esse vel mobiles poterit denegare? Quodsi recta ista videtur esse definitio, quod substantia rationabihter sensibilis et > mobilis anima dicatur, videtur haec eadem definitio etiam ad angelos pertinere. Quid enim aliud in ills quam sensus rationabilis et motus est? Quorum autem una definitionis ratio est, horum sine dubio et eadem substantia est. Paulus sane apostolus esse quendam -animalem hominem. significat, quem negat ‘ea quae sunt spiritus dei’ posse ‘recipere. sed “stultam- ei videri dicit spiritus sancti doctrinam, nec ‘posse eum intellegere quod spiritaliter discernatur. Sed et in alio loco ait -seminarl corpus animale. et “surgere corpus spiritale ostendens in resurrectione iustorum nihil animale futurum in his, qui vitam meruerint beatorum. Et ideo requirimus ne forte substantia aliqua sit, quae secundum hoc, quod anima est, inperfecta sit. Verum utrum propterea inperfecta sit, quod a perfectione decidit, an talis a deo facta sit, cum per ordinem singula discuti coeperint, requiremus. Si enim :animalis homo non recipit quae sunt spiritus dei, et pro eo, quod ‘animalis” est, melioris naturae, id est divinae, intellegentiam recipere non potest, hac fortasse de causa evidentius nos Paulus docere volens, quid sit per quod ‘ea, quae sunt spiritus. id est spiritalia, intellegere possimus, mentem magis quam animam spiritui sancto coniungit et sociat. Haec enim eum puto ostendere cum dicit: “Orabo spiritu, orabo et mente; psalmum dicam spiritui psalmum dicam et mente”. Et non dicit quia anima orabo, sed ‘spiritu et mente’; et non dicit: anima psallam, sed "spiritu psallam et mente”. 3. Bed fortasse requiritur: Si mens est, quae cum spiritu orat et psallit, et ipsa est, quae et perfectionem percipit et salutem, quomodo dicit Petrus: “Percipientes finem fidei nostrae salutem animarum nostrarum”? Si anima cum spiritu nec orat nec psallit, quomodo spera- . bit ‘salutem’? aut si T cum ad beatitudinem venerit, iam anima non dicetur? Sed videamus ne forte possit hoc modo responderi, quia sicut salvator venit ‘salvare quod perierat, et iam cum ue non est perditum quod prius perditum dicebatur: ita fortassis etiam hoe quod salvatur anima dicitur; eum autem iam salva facta fuerit, ex perfeetioris partis suae vocabulo nuncupabitur. Sed et illud adici posse videbitur quibusdam, quia sieut hoc, quod perditum est, erat sine dubio, antequam periret, cum aliud nescio quid erat quam perditum, sieut et erii utique cum iam non est perditum: ita etiam anima, quae perisse dieitur, videbitur fuisse quid aliquando, eum nondum perisset et propter hoe anima dieeretur, quae rursum ex perditione liberata potest iterum illud esse quod fuit, antequam periret et anima diceretur. Sed et ex ipsa nominis animae significatione, quam in graeco indieat, visum est nonnullis requirentibus curiosius posse non mediocrem suggeri intellectum. Nam sermo divinus ignem esse deum dixit, cum alt: “Deus noster ignis est consumens”. Sed et de angelorum substantia ita ait: “Qui facit angelos suos spiritus et ministros suos ignem urentem”, et alibi: “ Apparuit angelus domini in flamma ignis in rubo”. Insuper etiam mandatum accepimus, ut simus “spiritu ferventes’; per quod sine dubio igneum ostenditur et calidum dei verbum. Sed et Hieremias propheta audit ab eo, qui sibi responsa dabat: “Ecce dedi verba mea in os tuum, ignem”. Sicut ergo “deus ignis est’, et ‘angeli flamma ignis, et sancti quique ‘spiritu ferventes-: ita e contrario hi, qui deciderunt a dilectione dei, sine dubio refrixisse in caritate eius ae frigidi effecti esse dicendi sunt. Ait enim et dominus quia “pro eo quod multiplieata est iniquitas, refrigescet caritas multorum”. Sed et omnia ea, quaecumque sunt quae adversae potestati in scripturis sanetis conparantur, frigida semper invenies. Serpens: namque et “draco” diabolus dieitur: quorum quid frigidius invenitur? Sed et in aquis regnare dieitur draco, quod utique ad aliquem de malignis spiritibus retorquetur, et -in mari- eum propheta esse designat; et alibi dicit propheta quia “inducam gladium sanctum super draconem, serpentem fugientem, super draconem, serpentem perversum, et interficiet eum”; et iterum ait: “Etiam si abscesserint ab oculis meis et descenderint in profundum maris, ibi mandabo draconi et mordebit eos”. Sed et in lob ‘ipse rex esse omnium, quae in aquis sunts, dicitur. ‘A borea- vero ‘accendi mala super omnes, qui habitant terrame, propheta denuntiat. Boreas autem ventus in scripturis frigidus designatur, sicut seriptum est in Sapientia: “Frigidus ventus Borease. Quod et ipsum sine dubio de diabolo sentiendum est. Si ergo ea quidem, quae sancta sunt, ignis et lumen et ferventia nominantur, quae autem contraria sunt, frigida, et ‘caritas’ peccatorum dicitur ‘refrigescere’, requirendum est ne forte et nomen animae, quod graece dieitur a refrigescendo de statu diviniore ac meliore dietum sit et translatum inde, quod ex calore illo naturali et divino refrixisse videatur, et ideo in hoc quo nune est et statu et vocabulo sita sit. Denique propre laudabiliter animam poni in scripturis sanctis, require si facile invenias; culpabiliter autem frequenter occurrit, ut 101: “Anima mala perdit eum, qui possidet eam”, et “Anima quae peccat, ipsa morieture. Postea enim quam dictum est: “Omnes animae meae sunt, sicut anima patris ita anima fili meae sunt”, utique consequens videbatur ut diceret: Anima quae agit iustitiam, ipsa salvabitur et anima quae peccat, ipsa morletur. Sed nunc videmus quoniam quod eulpabile quidem est adiunxit ad animam, quod autem laude dignum erat reticuit. Videndum ergo est ne forte, sicut diximus ex ipso nomine declarari, ab eo quod refrixerit a fervore iustorum et divini ignis partieipatione ivy7, id est anima, appellata sit, nec tamen amisit facultatem restituendi se in illum statum fervoris, in quo ex initio fuit. Unde et propheta tale aliquid. videtur ostendere, ctim dicit: “Revertere, anima mea, in requiem tuam”. Ex quibus omnibus illud videtur ostendi, quod mens de statu ac dignitate sua declinans, effecta vel nuncupata est anima; quae si reparata fuerit et correcta, redit in hoc, ut sib mens. 4. Quod si ita est, decessus ipse mentis ac devolutio videtur mihi quod non aequalis omnium sentiendus sit, sed vel plus vel minus in animam verti, et aliquas quidem mentes servare aliquid etiam prioris vigoris, aliquas vero aut nihil aut perexiguum aliquid. Et inde est unde inveniuntur quidam statim ab ineunte aetate ardentioris acuminis, ali vero tardioris, nonnulli autem obtunsissimi et penitus indociles nasci. Verum tamen quod diximus mentem in animam verti vel si qua alia quae in hoe videntur aspicere, discutiat apud se qui legit diligentius et pertractet; a nobis tamen non putentur velut dogmata esse prolata, sed tractandi more ac requirendi discussa. Addat autem et hoc qui legit ad tractatum, quod etiam de salvatoris anima ex his quidem, quae in evangelio scripta sunt, observatur quod alia sunt quae ei sub animae nomine adseribuntur, et alia quae sub spiritus nomine deputantur. Nam cum passionem aliquam vel conturbationem sui vult indicare, sub nomine animae indicat, cum dicit: “Nune anima mea turbata est” et “Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem” et “Nemo tollit a me animam meam, sed ego pono eam abs me”. ‘Jn manus- autem “patris commendat- non animam sed “spiritum-, et cum “carnem- dicat ‘infirmam-, non dicit animam promptam esse sed ‘spiritum’; unde videtur quasi medium quiddam esse anima inter -carnem infirmam- et ‘spiritum promptum-. 5. Sed fortassis occurrat nobis aliquis ex his, de quibus ipsi in nostris propositionibus admonuimus, et dicat: Quomodo ergo etiam “dei anima- dieitur? Cui respondebimus hoe modo: Quia sicut omnia, quae corporaliter de deo dicuntur, id est vel digiti vel manus vel brachia vel oeuli vel os vel pedes, dicimus non haec humana membra, sed virtutes eius quasdam in his corporeorum membrorum appellationibus indicari: ita et esse aliquid aliud putandum est, quod appellatione hae, quae ‘anima dei’ dicitur, indicatur. Et si fas est audere nos in tali re amplius aliquid dicere, potest fortasse ‘anima dei- intellegi unigenitus filius eius. Sicut enim anima per omne corpus inserta movet omnia et agit atque operatur universa: ita et unigenitus filius dei, qui est verbum et sapientia eius, pertingit et pervenit ad omnem virtutem dei, insertus ei. Et fortassis ob huius sacramenti indicium corpus in seripturis vel dicitur deus vel describitur. Considerandum sane est, ne forte possit etiam pro hoc -anima dei- intellegi unigenitus eius, quoniam venit et ipse ‘in locum hune adflictationis- et ‘in convallem fletus descendit- et in locum humiliationis nostrae, sicut dicit in psalmo: “Quoniam humiliasti nos in loco adflietionise. Denique scio quosdam exponentes illud, quod in evangelio a salvatore dictum est: “Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem”, interpretatos esse de apostolis, quos velut meliores a reliquo corpore -animam suam- dixerit. Nam quia multitudo eredentium -eorpus- ilhus dicitur, apostolos velut a reliqua multitudine meliores -animam- eius intellegi debere dixerunt. Haee prout potuimus de rationabih anima discutienda magis a legentibus quam statuta ac definita protulimus. De animabus vero pecudum ceterorumque mutorum sufficiant illa, quae absolute superius diximus.
pass_a_gloss: After these things, the order now demands that we also inquire about the soul in general and, starting from the lower things, ascend to the higher things. For it is not doubted by anyone that there are souls in each and every animal, even in those that live in the waters, because both the common opinion of all people preserves this and the confirmation of the authority of holy scripture is added, when it is said that God made the great sea creatures and every soul of creeping animals, which the waters produced according to their kind. This is also confirmed by the common understanding of reason, even by those who define the soul with certain words. For the soul is defined in this way, that it is a substance and, although it is not explained as precisely in Latin, it can nevertheless be said to be 'sensible and movable'. This definition of the soul is also fittingly shown to be convenient for all animals and even for those that live in the waters, but also for insects. Scripture also adds the authority of another opinion, when it says: 'You shall not eat blood, because the soul of all flesh is its blood, and you shall not eat the soul with the flesh'; in which it is most clearly indicated that 'blood' is the soul of all animals. Now, if someone asks, since it is said that 'the soul of all flesh is its blood', how this can be said of bees and wasps and ants, but also of those that live in the waters, oysters or shellfish, and whatever other animals lack blood and are nevertheless clearly shown to be living things: it must be responded that in these kinds of living things, the power of red blood is had in that humor which is in them, although it is of a different color; for it does not matter what the color is, as long as the substance is vital. Concerning beasts of burden and cattle, there is no doubt among the common people that they are living things. This is also clearly shown by the sentence of divine scripture, when God says: 'Let the earth produce a living soul according to its kind, quadrupeds and creeping things and beasts of the earth according to their kind'. Now, concerning man, although there is no doubt and no one can ask, scripture nevertheless indicates that 'God breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul'. It remains to inquire about the angelic order, whether they have souls or are souls, or about the other divine and heavenly powers, but also about the contrary powers. We do not find any authority of divine scripture that angels or any divine spirits, ministers of God, are said to have souls or to be called souls; however, they are thought by many to be living things. Concerning God, we find it written that 'I will put my soul over the soul that eats blood, and I will destroy it from my people'. And elsewhere: 'I do not accept your new moons and sabbaths and great days; I hate your fasting and festivals and feast days, my soul hates them'. And in the twenty-first psalm, concerning Christ (for it is certain that this psalm is ascribed to him, as the gospel testifies), it is said: 'But you, Lord, do not withdraw your help, look to my defense, rescue my soul from the sword and my life from the power of the dog'. Although there are many other testimonies about the soul of Christ in the flesh. But the reason of the incarnation removes all question about the soul of Christ; for just as he truly had flesh, so he truly had a soul. Concerning what is called 'the soul of God' in the scriptures, it is difficult to understand and express; for we profess that nature to be simple and without any mixture of addition. Nevertheless, it seems that 'the soul of God' is named in the scriptures; concerning Christ, however, there is no doubt. And therefore it does not seem absurd to me to say or think something similar even about the holy angels and the other heavenly powers, if indeed that definition of the soul seems to apply also to them. For who can reasonably deny that they are sensible and movable? If this definition seems correct, that a substance is called a soul because it is rationally sensible and movable, then this same definition seems to apply also to angels. What else is there in them but rational sense and motion? And those things that have one definition are without doubt of the same substance. The apostle Paul indeed indicates that there is a certain 'animal man', whom he says cannot 'receive the things that are of the spirit of God', and says that 'the doctrine of the holy spirit seems foolish to him, and he cannot understand what is discerned spiritually'. But in another place, he says that 'it is sown an animal body and rises a spiritual body', showing that in the resurrection of the just, there will be nothing animal in those who have merited the life of the blessed. And therefore we ask whether perhaps there is some substance that is imperfect because it is a soul, according to what it is. But whether it is imperfect because it has fallen from perfection, or whether it was made such by God, we will inquire when we have begun to discuss each thing in order. For if the 'animal man' does not receive the things that are of the spirit of God, and because he is 'animal', he cannot receive the understanding of a better nature, that is, the divine, perhaps for this reason Paul wants to teach us more clearly what it is through which we can understand 'the things that are of the spirit', that is, spiritual things; he joins the mind rather than the soul to the holy spirit and associates it with him. For I think he shows this when he says: 'I will pray with the spirit, I will pray also with the mind; I will sing a psalm with the spirit, I will sing a psalm also with the mind'. And he does not say 'I will pray with the soul', but 'with the spirit and with the mind'; and he does not say 'I will sing a psalm with the soul', but 'I will sing a psalm with the spirit and with the mind'. But perhaps it is required to ask: If the mind is that which prays and sings with the spirit, and it is that which receives perfection and salvation, how does Peter say: 'Receiving the end of our faith, the salvation of our souls'? If the soul does not pray or sing with the spirit, how can it hope for salvation? Or if it comes to blessedness, will it no longer be called a soul? But let us see if perhaps it can be responded to in this way, that just as the savior came to save what was lost, and now that it is not lost, what was previously lost is no longer said to be lost: so perhaps also what is saved is called a soul; but when it has been saved, it will be called by the name of a more perfect part of itself. But also this can be added, that just as what is lost was certainly something before it was lost, and it was something else, I do not know what, than what is lost: so also what is saved will certainly be something when it is no longer lost; and thus the soul, which is said to have perished, seems to have been something at some time, before it perished, and for this reason it was called a soul, and it can again be what it was before it perished and be called a soul. But also from the very meaning of the name 'soul', which is indicated in Greek, it seems to some who inquire more curiously that a not insignificant understanding can be suggested. For the divine word said that God is a fire, when it says: 'Our God is a consuming fire'. But also concerning the substance of angels, it says: 'Who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire', and elsewhere: 'The angel of the Lord appeared in a flame of fire in a bush'. Moreover, we have also received the command to be 'fervent in spirit'; through which it is without doubt shown that the word of God is fiery and hot. And also the prophet Jeremiah hears from him who gave him responses: 'Behold, I have put my words in your mouth, a fire'. Just as, therefore, 'God is a fire', and 'angels are a flame of fire', and 'the holy ones are fervent in spirit': so, on the contrary, those who have fallen from the love of God are without doubt said to have grown cold in his charity and to have become cold. For the Lord says that 'because iniquity has multiplied, the charity of many will grow cold'. And all those things that are compared to the contrary power in the holy scriptures, you will always find to be cold. The serpent, namely, and 'the dragon', the devil, are called cold; what is colder than these can be found? But also it is said that the dragon reigns in the waters, which is certainly turned to one of the malignant spirits, and 'in the sea' the prophet indicates that it is; and elsewhere the prophet says that 'I will bring my holy sword upon the dragon, the fleeing serpent, upon the dragon, the perverse serpent, and I will kill it'; and again he says: 'Even if they have gone away from my eyes and descended into the depths of the sea, I will command the dragon and it will bite them'. And also in Job, it is said that 'the king of all things that are in the waters' is the devil. The prophet announces that 'the north wind' will kindle evils upon all who inhabit the earth; the north wind, however, is designated as cold in the scriptures, as it is written in Wisdom: 'The cold wind of the north'. This is without doubt to be understood concerning the devil. If, therefore, those things that are holy are called fire and light and fervent, and those things that are contrary are called cold, and 'the charity of sinners' is said to 'grow cold', it must be inquired whether perhaps the name 'soul', which is said in Greek, was said and transferred from a more divine and better state, because it seems to have grown cold from that natural and divine heat, and therefore it is now in this state and name. Finally, it is required to see if you can easily find that the soul is placed in the holy scriptures in a laudable way; but it is frequently found in a culpable way, as in 'A bad soul destroys its owner', and 'The soul that sins will die'. For after it was said: 'All souls are mine, as the soul of the father, so the soul of the son is mine', it seemed to follow that it would be said: 'The soul that does justice will save itself, and the soul that sins will die'. But now we see that what is culpable is added to the soul, and what is worthy of praise is omitted. Therefore, it must be seen whether perhaps, as we said, the soul is called from the fact that it has grown cold from the fervor of the just and the participation in the divine fire, and yet it has not lost the ability to restore itself to that state of fervor in which it was from the beginning. Whence also the prophet seems to show something similar, when he says: 'Return, my soul, to your rest'. From all these things, it seems to be shown that the mind, having fallen from its state and dignity, has been made or called a soul; which, if it is repaired and corrected, returns to being a mind. If this is so, the very falling away of the mind and its deviation seems to me to be something that should not be understood as equal for all, but rather as more or less turned into a soul, and some minds preserve something of their prior vigor, while others preserve nothing or very little. And from this, it is the case that some are found to be more ardent and sharp from the beginning of their age, while others are slower, and some are born very dull and completely unteachable. But let whoever reads this discuss it more carefully and thoroughly; we do not think that these things have been proposed as dogmas, but rather as things to be discussed and inquired into. Let the reader also add this to the discussion, that even concerning the soul of the savior, it is observed from what is written in the gospel that some things are ascribed to him under the name of soul, and other things are assigned to him under the name of spirit. For when he indicates some passion or disturbance of himself, he indicates it under the name of soul, when he says: 'Now my soul is troubled' and 'My soul is sorrowful even unto death' and 'No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down of myself'. But when he 'commends his spirit into the hands of the Father', he does not say 'soul' but 'spirit'; and when he says 'the flesh is weak', he does not say that the soul is ready, but 'the spirit'; whence it seems that the soul is something intermediate between 'weak flesh' and 'ready spirit'. But perhaps someone will occur to us from those things that we have warned about in our propositions, and will say: How, then, is 'the soul of God' said? To which we will respond in this way: Just as all those things that are said of God in a bodily way, that is, fingers or hands or arms or eyes or mouth or feet, we say that these are not human members, but rather certain powers of God that are indicated by the names of bodily members: so also it must be thought that there is something else that is indicated by the name 'soul of God'. And if it is permissible for us to dare to say something more about this, perhaps 'the soul of God' can be understood as the only-begotten Son of God. For just as the soul is inserted through the whole body and moves and acts and operates all things: so also the only-begotten Son of God, who is the Word and the wisdom of God, reaches and comes to every power of God, inserted into it. And perhaps for this reason, the body is said or described as God in the scriptures. It must be considered whether perhaps 'the soul of God' can also be understood as the only-begotten Son of God, because he came into this place of affliction and descended into the valley of tears, just as it is said in the psalm: 'For you have humbled us in the place of affliction'. Finally, I know that some interpreters have explained what was said by the savior in the gospel: 'My soul is sorrowful even unto death', as referring to the apostles, whom he called his 'soul', as if they were the better part of his body. For since the multitude of believers is called his 'body', they said that the apostles should be understood as his 'soul', as the better part of the multitude. We have proposed these things about the rational soul more for the readers to discuss than as established and defined dogmas. Concerning the souls of beasts and other mute animals, let what we have said above suffice.

pass_b_english: After considering these things, we are now compelled to investigate the soul in general, starting from the lower creatures and ascending to the higher ones. It is not doubted by anyone that every animal, even those living in water, possesses a soul, as both the common opinion of all people and the authority of holy scripture confirm, when it says that God created the great sea creatures and every soul of creeping animals, which the waters produced according to their kind (Genesis 1:21). This is also supported by the common understanding of reason, even by those who define the soul with specific words. The soul is defined as a substance that is sensible and movable, a definition that applies not only to all animals but also to those living in water and even insects. Scripture also adds another perspective, saying, 'You shall not eat blood, because the soul of all flesh is its blood, and you shall not eat the soul with the flesh' (Leviticus 17:11), clearly indicating that blood is the soul of all animals. If someone asks how this can be applied to bees, wasps, ants, and aquatic animals like oysters or shellfish, which lack blood yet are living things, the response would be that in these creatures, the power of red blood is present in the humor within them, regardless of its color, as long as the substance is vital. There is no doubt among the common people that beasts of burden and cattle are living things, a fact also evident from divine scripture, which says, 'Let the earth produce a living soul according to its kind, quadrupeds and creeping things and beasts of the earth according to their kind' (Genesis 1:24). Concerning humans, although there is no doubt, scripture still indicates that God breathed into man's face the breath of life, and man became a living soul (Genesis 2:7). The question remains regarding the angelic order, whether they have souls or are souls, or about other divine and heavenly powers, as well as contrary powers. We find no scriptural authority suggesting that angels or divine spirits, ministers of God, have souls or are called souls, though many consider them living things. Regarding God, scripture says, 'I will put my soul over the soul that eats blood, and I will destroy it from my people' (Leviticus 17:11), and elsewhere, 'I hate your new moons and sabbaths and great days; my soul hates them' (Isaiah 1:14). In the psalm concerning Christ, it is said, 'But you, Lord, do not withdraw your help, look to my defense, rescue my soul from the sword and my life from the power of the dog' (Psalm 21:1). The reason for the incarnation removes all question about Christ's soul, for just as he truly had flesh, so he truly had a soul. The concept of 'the soul of God' in scriptures is difficult to understand and express, given the simplicity of God's nature. However, it does not seem absurd to consider something similar regarding holy angels and other heavenly powers, if the definition of the soul applies to them. For who can deny that they are sensible and movable? If the definition of a soul as a rationally sensible and movable substance is correct, it seems to apply to angels as well. The apostle Paul speaks of an 'animal man' who cannot receive the things of the spirit of God, indicating a distinction between the animal and spiritual aspects of human nature. Paul also discusses the resurrection, where the body is sown as animal but rises as spiritual, suggesting a transformation from the animal to the spiritual. This leads to the question of whether there is a substance that is imperfect because it is a soul, and whether this imperfection is due to a fall from perfection or if it was created such by God. The distinction between the mind and the soul is also noteworthy, as Paul associates the mind with the spirit, saying, 'I will pray with the spirit, I will pray also with the mind; I will sing a psalm with the spirit, I will sing a psalm also with the mind' (1 Corinthians 14:15). The relationship between the soul and salvation is another point of inquiry, as Peter says, 'Receiving the end of our faith, the salvation of our souls' (1 Peter 1:9), yet if the soul does not pray or sing with the spirit, how can it hope for salvation? Perhaps the soul, once saved, is no longer called a soul but takes on a more perfect name. The origin of the term 'soul' from the Greek, indicating a cooling or a fall from a more divine state, suggests that the soul may have been named because it has grown cold from the natural and divine heat. This perspective is supported by scriptural references to God as a consuming fire (Deuteronomy 4:24) and to angels as spirits and ministers of fire. The command to be fervent in spirit (Romans 12:11) and the prophet Jeremiah's words, 'Behold, I have put my words in your mouth, a fire' (Jeremiah 1:9), further emphasize the divine and heavenly as fiery and hot, contrasting with the coldness of those who have fallen from God's love. The soul, having fallen from its state and dignity, may be restored to its former fervor, as suggested by the prophet's plea, 'Return, my soul, to your rest' (Psalm 116:7). This restoration implies that the mind, once it has fallen and been called a soul, can return to being a mind if it is repaired and corrected. The falling away of the mind and its deviation into a soul seems not to be equal for all but rather varies in degree, with some minds preserving more of their prior vigor than others. The discussion of the soul of the Savior, as observed from the gospel, shows that some things are attributed to him under the name of soul, while others are under the name of spirit, indicating a distinction between the two. For instance, when indicating passion or disturbance, he uses the term 'soul,' as in 'My soul is troubled' (John 12:27) and 'My soul is sorrowful even unto death' (Matthew 26:38), but when commending his spirit into the Father's hands, he does not say 'soul' but 'spirit.' This distinction suggests that the soul may be something intermediate between the weak flesh and the ready spirit. The question of how 'the soul of God' can be understood is complex, given the spiritual nature of God. Perhaps 'the soul of God' can be understood as the only-begotten Son of God, who, like the soul in a body, moves and operates all things, being the Word and wisdom of God. This interpretation is supported by the scriptural description of God's body and the command to be fervent in spirit, implying a deep connection between the divine and the spiritual. Ultimately, the nature of the soul, whether human, animal, or divine, requires careful consideration and discussion, recognizing the distinctions and relationships between the soul, the spirit, and the mind, as well as the scriptural references that guide our understanding of these concepts.
